lessons.title: A joke and a room
lessons.description: Dean opens with a presidential joke and a piece of etymology. Together they show what ‘comrade’ does: it names a relation of people on the same side and the expectations that come with it.
objectives: State the three registers in which Dean uses ‘comrade’
Explain why Obama’s joke works only if he is not a comrade
Connect the etymology of camera to ‘supported cover’

sections.heading: Three readings of a joke
paragraphs: At the 2016 White House Correspondents’ Dinner, Barack Obama teased Bernie Sanders for distancing himself, adding that this is not something one does to one’s comrade. Dean offers three readings. It might be red-baiting, a reminder that Sanders called himself a socialist. It might be a reminder that Sanders was not a Democrat and so not Obama’s party comrade. Or Obama might be ironically casting himself as Sanders’s comrade—the role the right had long assigned him.

The third reading carries the point. Everyone in the room knew Obama did not share Sanders’s politics. The joke worked because it invoked a norm the audience understood: comrades share a political horizon, and so they can expect solidarity from each other. You do not distance yourself from your comrades.

sections.heading: Comrade as relation and expectation
paragraphs: From the joke Dean extracts her working definition. ‘Comrade’ indexes a political relation and a set of expectations for action toward a common goal. It stresses the sameness of those on the same side: whatever their differences, comrades stand together, and that binding collectivizes and directs action toward a shared future.

Throughout the book she uses the word in three registers at once: as a term of address, as a figure of political belonging, and as a carrier of expectations. For communists, the horizon that gives the relation its content is an egalitarian society freed from private property and organized by the free association and collective decisions of the producers.
sections.callout: A comrade is not a kind of person but a relation between people on the same side.

sections.heading: From chamber to supported cover
paragraphs: The word is older than socialism. In Romance languages it first named someone who shared a room; the French camarade referred to a barracks room shared by soldiers. All of these go back to the Latin camera, a room, chamber or vault.

Dean draws a structural lesson from the vault: it is a repeatable form that produces an inside separate from an outside and holds a space open for those beneath it. Sharing such a space generates closeness and an expectation of solidarity that divides one side from the other. Comradeship, she concludes, is a political relation of supported cover.

example.title: Work it through: who can you count on?
example.body: Imagine a tenants’ union in one building. Some neighbours sign a petition and are never seen again; others attend every meeting, cover each other’s door-knocking shifts and show up when one household faces eviction. Dean would say the second group has entered a relation with expectations attached—not because they are friends or share an identity, but because they are on the same side of the same fight.

lessons.distinction: Don’t read the etymology as an argument that comrades must be physically close or intimate. Dean uses the vault as a figure for a generic, repeatable structure that holds a political space open. Later chapters stress that comrades are often far apart, and that the relation differs from friendship and neighbourliness.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: Why, on Dean’s third reading, does Obama’s joke work?
options: Because Obama really was a member of a socialist party
Because everyone knew he did not share Sanders’s politics, so the norm of solidarity was being invoked ironically
Because Sanders had joined the Democratic Party
Because the audience did not know what ‘comrade’ meant
quiz.explanation: The joke relies on the shared understanding that comrades share a politics and owe each other solidarity—and that Obama was not Sanders’s comrade.

quiz.question: What does Dean take from the etymology of camera?
options: That comrades must live together
That the word was originally military and therefore authoritarian
That comradeship is a political relation of supported cover, an inside held open against an outside
That comrade is a Russian word
quiz.explanation: The vault produces and holds open a shared space; Dean calls comradeship a political relation of supported cover.

lessons.title: Those you can count on
lessons.description: Comrades are the people you can count on even when you disagree or dislike each other. Dean explains this through accountability and the psychoanalytic idea of the ego ideal.
objectives: Explain why Dean treats comradeship as instrumental and long-term
Describe accountability as seeing yourself through your comrades’ eyes
Distinguish the ego ideal from the ideal ego

sections.heading: An anchor, not an ad-hoc group
paragraphs: Comrades tie themselves together for a common purpose: if we want to win, we have to act together. Dean quotes Angela Davis explaining why she joined the Communist Party. Davis wanted an anchor and comrades who shared an ideology; she was tired of loose groups that fell apart at the first difficulty and knew the fight had to be waged collectively by an organization with permanence.
Dean’s gloss is simple: comrades are those you can count on. They share enough of a commitment to do more than one-off actions, and so together they can fight a long fight.

sections.heading: Accountable to each other
paragraphs: Comradeship is voluntary, but what it asks is not always what we would choose. Vivian Gornick’s interviews with former members of the CPUSA include a woman who hated selling papers and canvassing but did it anyway, because she could not have faced her comrades the next day. They were accountable to each other.

Being accountable means seeing your own actions through another’s eyes. Are you letting your comrades down, or doing work they would respect? The relation reaches back into each person and changes how they judge themselves.
sections.callout: Comrades can count on each other even when they don’t like each other.

sections.heading: Ego ideal versus ideal ego
paragraphs: Dean borrows a Lacanian distinction, via Žižek. The ideal ego is an imaginary self-image—how I would like to appear: the brilliant orator, the fearless militant. The ego ideal is symbolic: the point from which I observe and judge myself. In her earlier book Crowds and Party she treated the good comrade as an ideal ego; here she stresses the comrade as ego ideal.

This matters for the whole book. The comrade is less a portrait one tries to resemble than a perspective one adopts, produced by belonging to a side and working back on those who belong to it. Chapter One will later use the same distinction against the ally, who stays at the imaginary level.

example.title: Work it through: the Monday meeting
example.body: A volunteer is tired and would rather skip the Monday phone bank. What gets her there? Not an image of herself as a hero (ideal ego), but the thought of how the others will see her if she leaves them short-handed (ego ideal). The Accountability lab models this: participation that depends only on individual comfort decays, participation that responds to others’ presence can hold up.

lessons.distinction: ‘Accountable’ is easily heard as surveillance or guilt. Dean’s claim is narrower: shared commitment produces a perspective from which people evaluate their own work, and this is what makes long-term collective action possible. Whether that perspective becomes punitive is a question she takes up in chapters three and four.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: In Dean’s usage, what is the comrade as ego ideal?
options: The perspective from which party members assess their own work
An idealized image of oneself as a heroic militant
The party leader whom members imitate
A personal friend who gives advice
quiz.explanation: The ego ideal is the symbolic point from which one judges oneself; the ideal ego is the imaginary self-image.

quiz.question: Why did the woman Gornick interviewed keep selling papers she hated selling?
options: She was paid by the party
She feared expulsion
She believed selling papers was the most effective tactic
She could not have faced her comrades otherwise—they were accountable to each other
quiz.explanation: Her motive was accountability to her comrades, which Dean reads as the ego-ideal function of comradeship.

lessons.title: Horizon, party and common time
lessons.description: Dean places the comrade inside two larger arguments—communism as the horizon of left politics and the party as its necessary form—then shows how comradeship changes work, time and address.
objectives: Describe the negative and positive sides of the communist horizon
Summarize Dean’s case against the left’s rejection of the party
Explain how comradeship revalues work and time, and why address can be both joyful and disciplining

sections.heading: The communist horizon
paragraphs: To see the political horizon as communist is to foreground the struggle of the proletarianized against the determination of life by markets, value, a division of labour by sex and race, imperialism and neocolonialism. Dean finds this horizon in struggles against police violence, around pipelines and water, over debt and public services, and in LGBTQ fights against discrimination. It is international: a negation of the global capitalist present.

Communism also has a positive side: a system of production organized around social needs, collectively decided by the producers, and attentive to how people treat each other and the world. Building it takes more than resistance and riot.

sections.heading: Against ‘no party!’
paragraphs: Dean argues that thinkers as different as Negri and Badiou converge on rejecting the party, which is dismissed as authoritarian, outdated or unsuited to networks. She calls this thirty-year-old consensus a left dogmatism: it ignores what association does to those who struggle together and relies on a fantasy of the party as a totalitarian machine.

The movements of the squares in Greece and Spain, and the limits of Occupy, renewed interest in a form that can scale and outlast the crowd. A theory of the comrade contributes by looking past leaders and led to the effects of political belonging on everyone on the same side.
sections.callout: Comrade attends to what belonging does to those who belong—not only to who leads.

sections.heading: Work, time and the force of address
paragraphs: Comradeship revalues work. Echoing Marx’s line that under communism labour becomes life’s prime want, Dean says comrades want to do political work because they see its value through each other’s eyes. Against Bernard Aspe’s diagnosis of a lost ‘common time’—time enclosed and measured by apps and trackers—common struggle produces a collective change in capacities.

Address matters too. Frank Wilderson recalls beaming when Chris Hani called him comrade, and later addressing Nelson Mandela as comrade to remind him of the militancy he had shed. The same word welcomes and disciplines. Discipline and joy are two sides of one coin, and comrade works as a utopian form in Kathi Weeks’s sense: it estranges us from the present and opens hope for the future.

example.title: Work it through: an ordinary week
example.body: Count the hours in a week that belong to anyone but the boss or the feed: commute, shifts, scrolling. Now add a weekly union meeting, a shared meal after a picket, a reading group. Dean’s claim is not that these hours are more pleasant, but that they are common: time produced and enjoyed together, outside capitalist measurement.

lessons.distinction: Dean is not saying every left organization should become a Leninist vanguard overnight, nor that parties are free of the problems critics name. Her target is the reflexive dismissal of the party form, which she thinks prevents the left from learning from a century of organizers’ experience.

furtherReading.label: Marx · Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875)

quiz.question: What does Dean call the left’s thirty-year rejection of the party form?
options: A necessary correction to Stalinism
A healthy pluralism
A left dogmatism that has gotten us nowhere
An unavoidable effect of the internet
quiz.explanation: She calls rejection of the party the left’s dogmatism of the last thirty years.

quiz.question: What does Wilderson’s address to Mandela as ‘comrade’ illustrate?
options: That comrade is only a polite greeting
That the word’s equalizing insistence can also be a disciplining reminder of what is expected
That Mandela rejected communism
That comrade was banned in South Africa
quiz.explanation: Calling Mandela ‘comrade’ stitched him back into the militancy he had shed: address can impose expectations.

lessons.title: Survivors and systems
lessons.description: Two opposite tendencies dominate contemporary left culture, Dean argues: attachment to survivor identities and fascination with vast systems. Both make class struggle unintelligible.
objectives: Describe the survivor and system tendencies
Link them to neoliberalism and communicative capitalism
Explain why Dean says the pair yields a left devoid of politics

sections.heading: Two tendencies
paragraphs: On one side are survivors: people left with nothing to cling to but identities forged in struggles to survive, often attached to the pain of those struggles. This emphasis appears on social media, in universities and in some activist networks, voiced through identity and appeals to allyship.

On the other side are systems: geology, extinction, algorithms, ‘hyperobjects’, processes so vast that we can barely conceive of them, let alone affect them. This emphasis dominates aesthetic and theoretical venues. Accounts of systems tend to have no survivors in them; when people appear, they appear as the problem.

sections.heading: Neoliberalism’s displacement of politics
paragraphs: Dean ties both tendencies to neoliberal dismantling of social institutions and to the networked, personalized media she calls communicative capitalism. Jobs, unions, housing and schools have become insecure, while ideology describes this as choice and personal responsibility.

Carl Schmitt said liberalism replaced politics with ethics and economics. Dean proposes a neoliberal variant: responsibilized individuals on one side, determining systems on the other. Sociologist Jennifer Silva’s interviews with working-class young adults show how survival, against the odds and alone, can become the very core of a dignified identity.
sections.callout: Survivors persist in unlivable conditions; systems are watched and mourned. Neither is changed.

sections.heading: A left devoid of politics
paragraphs: Both tendencies, Dean argues, make class struggle—divisive struggle over common conditions for an egalitarian future—unintelligible. In its place we get either the fragmenting assertion of particular survival or an obsession with the coming impossibility of anyone surviving.

The comrade is her alternative to both. It is neither a unique survivor nor a speck within an impersonal process, but one of many on the same side, whose collective capacity is the missing middle term.

example.title: Work it through: two headlines
example.body: One post tells a personal story of getting through a medical debt crisis alone; another shares a chart of planetary carbon budgets with the caption ‘we’re doomed’. Dean would ask what is missing from both: an organized ‘we’ that could change the conditions—say, a campaign for public health care or a union fighting a fossil employer. The Scale lab lets you see that gap.

lessons.distinction: Dean does not deny that trauma is real or that planetary systems matter. Her claim is about political form: when these become the frames for left thought, they displace the question of collective agency. Critics reply that she underestimates how identity-based movements have built collective power.

furtherReading.label: Dean · The Anamorphic Politics of Climate Change (e-flux 69, 2016)

quiz.question: According to Dean, what do the survivor and system tendencies have in common?
options: Both are right-wing
Both reject social media
Both come from the Communist Party
Both render class struggle unintelligible
quiz.explanation: Each in its own way displaces the divisive collective struggle over common conditions.

quiz.question: How does Dean adapt Schmitt’s claim that liberalism replaces politics with ethics and economics?
options: Neoliberalism displaces politics into an opposition between responsibilized individuals (survivors) and determining systems
Neoliberalism restores politics through markets
Neoliberalism replaces economics with ethics
Neoliberalism abolishes the individual
quiz.explanation: Her version: self-reliant survivors on one side, impersonal systems on the other.

lessons.title: Four openings, one symptom
lessons.description: Despite the impasse, Dean sees four openings for politics. She then argues that the sense that ‘comrade’ sounds alien is a symptom of defeat, and that attachment to identity is a fantasy of wholeness.
objectives: List the four openings Dean identifies
Explain why the strangeness of ‘comrade’ is symptomatic rather than descriptive
Distinguish identities as sites of struggle from grounds of struggle

sections.heading: Number, identity, the generic, the party
paragraphs: First, communicative capitalism runs on number—big data, followers, shares—and movements too invoke the many; the power of the people lies in the many over the few, if they organize. Second, identity is losing its ability to ground left politics: no political conclusion follows from an identity, and the right increasingly runs its own identity politics.

Third, the flood of demands on attention has produced generic shortcuts—hashtags, memes—that let local struggles see themselves as instances of something larger. Fourth, movements have hit the limits of horizontality and allyship, prompting renewed interest in parties and in organizing the many.

sections.heading: Why ‘comrade’ sounds jarring
paragraphs: In the US the term can seem alien; in Europe, too Stalinist. Dean grants this some merit but reads it historically: the hesitation reflects the defeat of the Soviet Union, intense neoliberalization and a cult of individual identity in a post-political setting.

What the left has celebrated—the personal as the privileged site of politics—is for Dean the symptom of its defeat: the erosion of working-class power and its parties. That ‘comrade’ doesn’t ring true describes a problem to be solved and an organization to be built.
sections.callout: The sense that ‘comrade’ is out of place is evidence of what has been lost, not of what is impossible.

sections.heading: Identity: a site, not a ground
paragraphs: When identity is all that is left, holding on to it makes sense: at least one survives. But Silva found that attachment to survivor identity can leave people unable to criticize the conditions they struggle under, so that survival itself looks like the political achievement.

Dean calls this attachment pathological in a psychoanalytic sense: an attachment to a fantasy of wholeness, a pure position guaranteeing that we are right. Identities are split and contested—sites of class struggle. That someone is a woman, black, transgender or a survivor tells us nothing about their politics.

example.title: Work it through: a hashtag
example.body: A hashtag about a local water crisis spreads to dozens of cities facing contaminated supplies. Nobody reads every post, but the shared name lets people see their tap water as one case of a larger pattern. That is Dean’s third opening: the generic as a container for many particular contents—a first step toward the generic comrade.

lessons.distinction: Saying identities are ‘sites, not grounds’ is not saying they are unreal or unimportant. Dean’s point is that political conclusions must be built through struggle and cannot be read off a category; chapter two shows how the CPUSA fought oppression by race and sex without making identity the basis of belonging.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of Dean’s four openings?
options: The power of number in communicative capitalism
A return of stable national identities that can ground left politics
Generic markers such as hashtags and memes
Movements hitting the limits of horizontality and allyship
quiz.explanation: Her second opening is the opposite: identity is losing its ability to ground a left politics, and nationalism is the right’s identity politics.

quiz.question: What does Dean mean by calling identities sites rather than grounds of struggle?
options: Identities should be abolished immediately
Identities determine politics
Identities are split and contested, so no politics follows automatically from them
Identities matter only online
quiz.explanation: An identity tells us nothing about someone’s politics; politics has to be built.

lessons.title: The ally as symptom
lessons.eyebrow: Chapter One · From Allies to Comrades · §§14–16
lessons.description: Dean reads popular how-to-be-an-ally guides as lifestyle manuals that turn politics into self-work. The ally is hierarchical, specific and acquiescent; the comrade is egalitarian, generic and utopian.
objectives: Describe the ‘field of operation’ the ally guides imagine
Explain ‘punishment without discipline’
Distinguish practical alliances from allyship as a model of politics

sections.heading: Allyship as a lifestyle manual
paragraphs: In US activist circles an ally is usually a privileged person who wants to help the oppressed. The guides that circulate online insist that allyship is a process, not an identity, and give lists of dos and don’ts. Dean compares them to decluttering books and clean-eating tips: techniques for navigating a neoliberal environment of privilege and oppression.

Their imagined field of action is social media, donations, hiring, campus conversations and sometimes protests—but above all the ally’s own feelings and attitudes. Reading one guide, Dean notes that struggles are treated like possessions the ally takes on while being told they have no right to them; what the politics actually is remains unstated.

sections.heading: Imaginary allies, punishment without discipline
paragraphs: One guide says the more uncomfortable and defensive you feel, the more likely you are on the right track. Dean reads this as an act of the self on the self: the ally is imaginary, an ideal ego, not a symbolic ego ideal. The space for politics shrinks, so the ally acts on what is left—social media and themselves.

The injunction to educate yourself makes learning a solitary act of consumption, cut off from discussion or a political tradition. The would-be ally can be scolded, but no one is responsible for guidance: punishment without discipline. ‘Ally’ is not a term of address; it marks a limit—you will never be one of us. And the advice to focus on those who share your identity treats identities as fixed little sovereign states.
sections.callout: Where the ally is hierarchical, specific and acquiescent, the comrade is egalitarian, generic and utopian.

sections.heading: Alliances yes, allyship no
paragraphs: Dean is explicit that the left needs alliances. A struggle with communism as its horizon will involve tactical alliances among classes, sectors and tendencies, and allies may become comrades. Rejecting alliances would be absurd. What she rejects is allyship as the model for struggles against oppression and exploitation.

She closes with Mark Fisher’s call to relearn comradeship and solidarity instead of doing capital’s work by condemning each other. If attachment to individual identity is the form of our political incapacity, recognizing it opens collective capacities. Her examples will come mostly from the CPUSA: if even that individualist, racist, Cold War culture produced comrades, the form is available to us.

example.title: Work it through: two responses to a racist remark
example.body: At work, a manager makes a racist joke. The ally-guide response: privately examine your discomfort, decide not to centre yourself, perhaps post about it later. The comrade response Dean has in mind: raise it with co-workers, take it to the union, and act together so that no one faces retaliation alone. The first changes how one person feels; the second changes the relation of forces.

lessons.distinction: This chapter is polemical and selective: Dean analyses popular online guides, not the full literature on solidarity. Many organizers who use ‘ally’ mean something close to her ‘comrade’. Read her as attacking a model of politics—individual, attitudinal, identity-bound—rather than every person who uses the word.

furtherReading.label: Mark Fisher · Exiting the Vampire Castle (2013)

quiz.question: What does Dean mean by ‘punishment without discipline’?
options: The would-be ally can be scolded and shamed, but no one takes responsibility for concrete guidance or training
Allies are expelled from parties
Allies punish oppressors
Discipline is always a form of punishment
quiz.explanation: Telling someone to ‘Google it’ relieves the scolder of any duty to provide guidance; there is blame without a collective practice.

quiz.question: Which statement matches Dean’s position on alliances?
options: All alliances betray the working class
Allies and comrades are the same thing
The left should only work with people who share its identity
Tactical alliances are necessary, but allyship should not be the model for struggle
quiz.explanation: She calls rejecting alliances absurd; her target is allyship as the form and model of politics.

lessons.title: Comrade Woman
lessons.description: Is the comrade a man? Dean answers with history—Kollontai, Zetkin, the women of the CPUSA, the Mary Inman controversy—and then with theory: comrade is a container indifferent to its contents.
objectives: Explain Dean’s ‘speculative-compositive’ method
Summarize the historical case that comrades are women and women are comrades
Explain why Dean reads the masculinity worry as a fear of losing specificity

sections.heading: Scavenging the ruins
paragraphs: Chapter two answers the worry that comrade carries a masculine, white imaginary. Dean calls her method speculative-compositive: rather than a linear history or a critique of actually existing socialisms, she extracts examples and salvages them for present struggles, scavenging the ruins of communism for old hopes and lessons.

Her first answer is a list—Luxemburg, Davis, Kollontai, Claudia Jones, Zetkin and many more—but she notes that proper names miss the relational point. Better evidence is the mass of women in communist movements and the commissions, conferences and publications that organized them, such as the 1907 International Conference of Socialist Women and Lenin’s insistence to Zetkin that a woman communist is a party member with equal rights and duties.

sections.heading: Red feminism and the Inman affair
paragraphs: In the CPUSA, women reached 40 percent of members during the 1930s and parity in 1944. Following Engels, party pamphlets traced women’s subordination to private property and demanded equal pay, maternity insurance, free childcare and legal birth control. Black communist women such as Louise Thompson Patterson and Claudia Jones developed the theory of black women’s triple exploitation—as workers, as women and as black people.

Drawing on Kate Weigand’s Red Feminism, Dean revisits Mary Inman, who argued in 1940 that housework is productive labour. The party rejected the claim—Avram Landy answered that Marxism is a theory of exploitation, not of usefulness—yet leaders still treated Inman as a comrade. Dean argues that the later feminist story of a party hostile to women’s issues repeats Inman’s grievance more than the record.

sections.heading: A container indifferent to its contents
paragraphs: Perhaps, Dean suggests, the masculinity worry is really a fear of losing individual specificity—the fear Fredric Jameson saw in reactions to utopia. Comrade insists on the equalizing sameness of those on the same side and frees people from identities imposed by patriarchal racial capitalism.

This does not make sexism vanish: Robin D. G. Kelley notes that white women comrades were often confined to the mimeograph machine. But comrade introduces another possibility and a standard by which old ways are judged. It is not the two of love—lovers look at each other, comrades look together at a horizon—and it has what Lacan calls a non-all structure: anyone, but not everyone.
sections.callout: Comrade doesn’t abolish the antagonism of sex; it lets another relation intrude and judge it.

example.title: Work it through: who washes the dishes?
example.body: Dean cites a 1930s case where a male communist was removed from leadership for refusing to help with childcare. The point is not that the party was a feminist utopia, but that being comrades gave women a standard to hold men to: in the party, men and women were supposed to be equals, and could be called to account when they were not.

lessons.distinction: Dean’s history is deliberately selective and partisan. Historians of the CPUSA disagree about how far its commitments to women’s equality were practised, and the Inman case is still read in opposite ways (Dean sides with Weigand against the version repeated by Viewpoint Magazine in 2015). Keep the factual record and Dean’s interpretation apart.

furtherReading.label: Clara Zetkin · Lenin on the Women’s Question (1920)

quiz.question: What does Dean call her method in chapter two?
options: Dialectical materialist history
Deconstructive genealogy
Speculative-compositive: salvaging examples from their contexts for present struggles
Comparative statistics
quiz.explanation: She extracts examples and composes them into a case for the present rather than writing a linear history.

quiz.question: How did the party’s Avram Landy answer Inman’s claim that housework is productive labour?
options: Housework is useful, but Marxism is a theory of the exploitation of labour, not its usefulness
Housework should be paid by the state
Women should leave the home for factory work only
Housework is not labour at all
quiz.explanation: Landy granted usefulness but grounded women’s demands in their oppression as members of the working class.

lessons.title: The Black Comrade
lessons.description: Is the comrade white? Dean separates two suspicions and answers them through Lucy Parsons, Cyril Briggs, Wilderson and Claudia Jones—and through Briggs’s ‘acid test’ for white comrades.
objectives: Name the two suspicions behind the worry that comrade is white
Describe Cyril Briggs’s synthesis of black nationalism and Leninism
Explain the ‘acid test’ and what it demanded of white communists

sections.heading: Two suspicions
paragraphs: The worry that comrade is white ignores communist and anticolonial struggles from India and Vietnam to South Africa and the United States, and a large scholarship on black communism. Dean breaks the US worry into two suspicions: that black people cannot be comrades with each other, and that black and white people cannot be comrades.

The first assumes a racial kinship that leaves no room for political division among black people—clearly false. Read another way, it points to a black radical tradition irreducible to Marxism. Dean accepts that tradition and asks why some of its figures turned to communism: Lucy Parsons put class first, and Cyril Briggs, founder of the Crusader and the African Blood Brotherhood, fused race-first politics with Leninist internationalism.

sections.heading: Practising social equality
paragraphs: In Jabu’s retort to Stimela—‘Brother,’ not ‘comrade’—Wilderson records the anguish that comradeship might be a ruse that subordinates black interests. Yet he also recalls a Soviet man taking his hand in the 1970s and thinking that if communism would cleanse his hands, he was a communist. Ernest Rice McKinney remembered white youths in Pittsburgh calling an interracial group ‘comrades’ because communists were known for practising social equality.

Practice often fell short: in 1949 Claudia Jones called out comrades for failing to extend courtesy to black women and to bring them into leadership. Dean’s point is that the expectation itself—held even by non-communists—was radical egalitarianism extending into everyday life.

sections.heading: Briggs’s acid test
paragraphs: Briggs warned that white ‘friendship’ had often been self-serving, yet argued that white workers needed black workers and that black and white had already fought together. He proposed an acid test: is a white person willing to see black people defend themselves with arms, even against white people? A 1932 organizer’s instructions told communists to be ready to die defending any black person’s rights.

Dean reads this as the condition of black–white comradeship: white communists had to give up their property in whiteness. Against narratives of manipulation and betrayal, she follows historians such as Kelley, Naison and Solomon in seeing the party, for a time, as the leading interracial organization against white supremacy.
sections.callout: Black–white comradeship required white comrades to prove they would defend black liberation to the end.

example.title: Work it through: the warehouse
example.body: Management offers a raise to one group of workers if they drop demands raised by another, more racialized group. Briggs’s point, translated: the white workers become comrades only by refusing the deal—by treating the others’ demands as their own even when it costs them. Solidarity is shown at the moment it is expensive.

lessons.distinction: Some readers, including writers Dean mentions such as Richard Wright and Harold Cruse, told the CPUSA’s relation to black Americans as a story of manipulation and disillusion. Dean sides with historians who reject that story, but she also records failures. Hold both: the ideal Dean defends and the evidence about how far it was realized.

quiz.question: What is Dean’s response to the existence of a black radical tradition independent of Marxism?
options: She denies it exists
She treats it as a branch of Marxism
She says it proves comrade is a white concept
She accepts it and asks how and why some black radicals turned to communism
quiz.explanation: The tradition supports her argument by showing figures like Briggs taking up communism on their own terms.

quiz.question: What was Cyril Briggs’s ‘acid test’ for white people?
options: Whether they would join the African Blood Brotherhood
Whether they would accept black people defending themselves with arms, even against white people
Whether they could quote Lenin
Whether they lived in Harlem
quiz.explanation: The test measured commitment to black self-defence and liberation, not sympathy.

lessons.title: The Black Belt thesis
lessons.eyebrow: Chapter Two · The Black Belt Thesis · §§26–27
lessons.description: Dean calls the Comintern’s line on black self-determination ‘scandalous’—and defends it. It put the black comrade in the position of ego ideal for the whole party.
objectives: State the Black Belt thesis and the nation-versus-race debate
Explain Haywood’s tactical argument for the self-determination line
Explain what it means that the black comrade became the party’s ego ideal

sections.heading: An oppressed nation?
paragraphs: After years of debate, the Comintern and the CPUSA adopted the position that black people in the Black Belt—a swathe of majority-black Southern counties—formed an oppressed nation with a right to self-determination. Dean calls the thesis scandalous because it is so often dismissed as dogmatic or absurd, and because it cuts against the assumption that communists subordinate everything to class.

Harry Haywood, its main architect, used Stalin’s four-part definition of a nation and a history running from slavery through the betrayal of Reconstruction to imperialism, which froze black Southerners in a landless, semi-slave position. Opponents, including black communists such as James Ford and Otto Hall, saw black Americans as an oppressed racial minority whose goal was assimilation; C. L. R. James also argued against the thesis.

sections.heading: Why the line mattered tactically
paragraphs: Haywood argued that treating oppression as racial prejudice detached racism from its socio-economic roots and reduced the struggle to a campaign against bad attitudes. The self-determination line instead made the black freedom struggle a revolutionary movement in its own right, an equal partner of the workers’ struggle against a common enemy.

It also gave the party a position from which to fight white chauvinism: white workers’ class consciousness would be mere race consciousness unless they committed to abolishing Jim Crow and lynching. As Mark Solomon put it, it redefined black–white cooperation on the basis of new power relations among equals.

sections.heading: The black comrade as ego ideal
paragraphs: For Dean, the thesis placed the black comrade in the position of ego ideal: white comrades now had to judge their actions as a black comrade would. The party ran self-criticism campaigns, cultivated black leaders, held public trials and expelled chauvinists, and refused concessions to segregation even at the price of isolation in the South.

She does not hide the cost. The campaign sometimes degenerated into fantastic accusations and was used in factional fights; the critical impulse turned on itself so fiercely that comradeship could look like an impossible ideal—a theme she returns to in chapter four.
sections.callout: Under racial capitalism, sameness has to be actively recomposed by confronting racism, not assumed.

example.title: Work it through: a union drive in a segregated town
example.body: In a town where black and white workers are kept apart, a union that treats racism as ‘a distraction from wages’ will lose black workers’ trust. One that makes ending segregation a core demand—even if some white workers walk—builds unity on new terms. That is the tactical logic Dean finds in Haywood.

lessons.distinction: Dean is not asking readers to adopt a 1928 programme. She uses the Black Belt thesis as an example of comradeship that refused to subordinate black liberation to class struggle. Whether the national framing was correct remains disputed, among communists then and historians now.

furtherReading.label: Harry Haywood · The Struggle for the Leninist Position on the Negro Question (1933)

quiz.question: Why does Dean call the Black Belt thesis ‘scandalous’?
options: Because it was secret
Because it is often dismissed as absurd and because it defies the idea that communists put class above every other struggle
Because it was written by Stalin alone
Because it called for black emigration to Africa
quiz.explanation: Both its common dismissal and its challenge to workerism make it ‘scandalous’ in her sense.

quiz.question: What tactical danger did Haywood see in treating black oppression only as racial prejudice?
options: It would anger the Comintern
It would make the party too radical
It would reduce the struggle to a campaign against attitudes, detached from its economic roots
It would split the Socialist Party
quiz.explanation: He thought the prejudice framing led to a reformist struggle against bad ideas rather than against the system.

lessons.title: The comrade as zero-level
lessons.eyebrow: Chapter Two · The Negativity of Comrade · §§28–30
lessons.description: Dean turns from positive content to negativity. In Platonov’s novel Chevengur, the destitute ‘others’ have nothing but each other—and that relation is the zero-level of communism.
objectives: Explain why Dean shifts from inclusion to the negativity of comrade
Describe Platonov’s prochie and their comradeship
Explain the contrast between Genosse and tovarish and how Dean resolves it

sections.heading: Taking a side
paragraphs: Some activists may feel no list of included identities can ever be enough. Dean answers with negativity: comrade means taking a side rather than denying that sides exist. Belonging to a side makes comrades indifferent to individual difference and equal with respect to belonging; it requires dissolving attachments to self-sufficiency, hierarchy and uniqueness.
Andrei Platonov’s Chevengur, completed in 1928, shows this best. Its comrades are not disciplined cadres but destitute masses who arrive in a steppe village that believes it has achieved communism.

sections.heading: The comradeship of the ‘others’
paragraphs: Platonov calls them prochie—the ‘others’ or ‘miscellaneous’, a word, Maria Chehonadskih explains, used on early Soviet forms when a person’s class could not be determined. Classless, propertyless, even without nationality, they pile together for warmth and have only each other. One Bolshevik sees in them true international proletarians: they aren’t anybody.

Their destitution produces not isolated egoists but comradeship as the minimal relation needed to go on. Isabelle Garo describes Platonov’s communism as a world that doesn’t exist, could be built and is already in ruins; comrade is the relation that exists in and as the absence of property, nationality and recognizable identity.

sections.heading: Enjoyment and the commodity
paragraphs: The German Genosse is linked to geniessen, to enjoy, and to shared use; the Russian tovarish to tovar, a commodity. Platonov seems to side against property: when nothing lies between people, they stop parting and keep each other warm. But in one scene the others carefully keep flies off each other, as the bourgeoisie once guarded their houses and livestock.

Dean reads this as a collective self-possession of the unpropertied: comrades as each other’s only wealth, enjoying each other rather than letting property take the other’s place. Via Žižek, the zero-level appears only retroactively, from the standpoint of a new political intervention. From the perspective of communism, desolation is an opening.
sections.callout: The comrade is what remains when everything else is gone—and the point from which something new can start.

example.title: Work it through: a strike kitchen
example.body: During a long strike, savings run out and families pool food in a shared kitchen. Status at work, seniority and neighbourhood rivalries matter less; what matters is that everyone eats and no one breaks ranks. Dean’s ‘zero-level’ names this relation of people who have, for now, only each other—and who discover a capacity they did not have alone.

lessons.distinction: Dean is not romanticizing poverty or saying hunger makes people comrades. Platonov’s comradeship is melancholic, and the zero-level is visible only from the standpoint of a political project that reads destitution as an opening. Without that project, destitution is just destitution.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: Who are Platonov’s prochie?
options: The classless, propertyless ‘others’ whose class identity could not be determined
The Bolshevik leaders of Chevengur
Wealthy peasants expelled from the village
Foreign soldiers
quiz.explanation: The word marked people whose class was unknowable—remnants with nothing but each other.

quiz.question: How does Dean resolve the apparent opposition between Genosse (enjoyment) and tovarish (commodity)?
options: She rejects the Russian word entirely
She says comrades should own property in common
She says both words are military
The unpropertied possess and enjoy each other—comrades as each other’s only wealth
quiz.explanation: Swatting flies off each other, the others show a collective self-possession: things (tovary) enjoying (geniessen) each other.

lessons.title: Thesis One: sameness, equality, solidarity
lessons.description: Political theory has princes, citizens and friends but no account of the comrade. Dean builds one, starting from Kollontai and Gorky: comrade is a generic, egalitarian and utopian relation.
objectives: Explain why the comrade is absent from political theory
Summarize what Kollontai and Gorky contribute
State Thesis One and what ‘utopian’ means in it

sections.heading: A missing figure
paragraphs: Political theory has studied the prince, citizen, neighbor, friend and enemy, master and slave—but not the comrade. In US philosophy, Dean suggests, this may be a legacy of McCarthyism, after which political philosophy returned only with Rawls. Socialist theory also lacks it, perhaps because it offers no theology of sovereignty or myth of origins, only histories of struggle, splits and schisms.
Two exceptions offer an affective opening rather than a theory: the Bolshevik Alexandra Kollontai and the writer Maxim Gorky.

sections.heading: Kollontai, Gorky and the queer comrade
paragraphs: For Kollontai, comradeship is a feeling of belonging among free and equal workers and the core of proletarian morality. Capitalism makes workers competitive and afraid; in place of the egoistic family a great family of workers will appear, in which all, men and women, are above all comrades. Gorky’s story ‘Comrade’ shows the word itself lifting a miserable city: the beggar and the prostitute who hear it stop submitting.

The early-1900s US magazine The Comrade, inspired by Whitman’s ‘love of comrades’, imagined relations that broke family, heteropatriarchy and binary gender; Rodchenko wanted things themselves to be comrades. In Chinese, tongzhi (comrade) also means gay—Hongwei Bao calls it intrinsically queer. Fanon closes The Wretched of the Earth addressing his readers as comrades; Orwell found everyone calling each other comrade in revolutionary Barcelona.

sections.heading: Thesis One
paragraphs: Comrade names a relation characterized by sameness, equality and solidarity. For communists this relation is utopian: it cuts through the determinations of capitalist society, marking the division between the miserable world we have and the egalitarian world to come.

Dean’s wager is that a speculative-compositive account—distilling what is common across many uses of the word—gives a view of political relation we need now, in a nationalist, competitive and exhausted world. Comrades are more than survivors and more than allies.
sections.callout: Thesis One: comrade = sameness, equality, solidarity—utopian because it cuts through capitalist determinations.

example.title: Work it through: the honorific test
example.body: Orwell noticed that in Barcelona nobody said ‘Señor’ or ‘Don’. Try it: in your workplace or school, which titles mark rank—‘boss’, ‘sir’, ‘doctor’? Imagine them replaced by one word used by everyone on the same side. Thesis One claims that this small linguistic change carries a large utopian charge, because it refuses hierarchy in the act of address.

lessons.distinction: ‘Utopian’ here is not an insult meaning ‘unrealistic’. Following Kathi Weeks (chapter one), Dean uses it for forms that estrange us from the present and open hope for a different future. The sameness in question is sameness with respect to a side, not uniformity of persons.

quiz.question: Why does Dean think the comrade is missing from socialist theory itself?
options: Socialists considered the word vulgar
The term was banned under Stalin
Socialist thought offers no theology of sovereignty or origin story, only histories of struggle and splits
Marx never used the word
quiz.explanation: She suggests socialism focuses on conflict and parties born of splits rather than foundational figures.

quiz.question: What does the Chinese tongzhi example show?
options: That comrade was always a military rank
That comrade can open kinship to new relations among strangers who share a politics—Bao calls it intrinsically queer
That the Chinese party abolished the word
That comrade only applies to men
quiz.explanation: Tongzhi replaces hierarchical, gendered designations and, in contemporary usage, also means gay.

lessons.title: Thesis Two: anyone but not everyone
lessons.description: Garbo’s envoy in Ninotchka cannot be recognized by her looks. Comradeship is open to anyone—but not to everyone, because it presupposes a division and a side.
objectives: Explain the Ninotchka scene as an argument
State why comradeship is both a relation and a division
Distinguish Dean’s comrade from Schmitt’s friend–enemy and from comrades in arms

sections.heading: Who is the comrade?
paragraphs: In Lubitsch’s Ninotchka (1939), three Soviet trade officials wait at a Paris station for the comrade Moscow has sent. One man looks like a comrade—until he greets someone with ‘Heil Hitler!’ The envoy turns out to be a woman, Garbo’s Nina Yakushova, who tells them not to make an issue of her womanhood: they are all there to work.
Dean draws two lessons. You can’t identify a comrade by appearance: identity has nothing to do with it. And not everyone is a comrade: some people are enemies.

sections.heading: Relation and division
paragraphs: ‘Anyone but not everyone’ means comradeship presupposes struggle and a division into sides. Comrades are the same with respect to that division. Yet unlike Carl Schmitt’s politics of friend and enemy, comradeship does not concern the enemy: the enemy is the setting, not what defines the relation between comrades.

Sartre wrote that comrades in arms’ brotherly love is the reverse of their hatred of the enemy. Dean distinguishes the socialist comrade: its solidarity is not inverted hatred but a response to fragmentation, hierarchy, isolation and oppression.
sections.callout: Thesis Two: anyone can be a comrade, but not everyone—comradeship is a relation that is also a division.

sections.heading: A space of possibility and non-belonging
paragraphs: Because anyone can be a comrade, the relation is open: someone unknown may turn out to be one. Because not everyone is, it also creates a space of non-belonging that is not the same as enmity.
That you are not my comrade does not make you my enemy. You may be a bystander, someone disengaged, an ally whose interests temporarily overlap with mine, or someone who will become a comrade later.

example.title: Work it through: the picket line
example.body: A stranger joins a picket and hands out coffee: anyone can be a comrade. A manager walks through the line: not everyone is. A passer-by who honks in support is neither enemy nor comrade—an ally, perhaps a future comrade. Thesis Two sorts these positions without reference to anyone’s identity.

lessons.distinction: Don’t equate ‘not everyone’ with a hostile friend–enemy politics. Dean explicitly distinguishes the comrade from Schmitt’s friend: the side is defined by commitment to a struggle, and the outside includes many people who are not enemies at all.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: What does the man at the station who says ‘Heil Hitler!’ demonstrate?
options: You cannot tell who is a comrade by looking; and some people are not comrades but enemies
That comrades must wear uniforms
That Soviet officials were incompetent
That the film is anti-communist
quiz.explanation: Appearance identifies nothing, and the division into sides is real.

quiz.question: According to Dean, someone who is not my comrade is…
options: Necessarily my enemy
A traitor
Always a member of another party
Possibly a bystander, an ally, or a future comrade
quiz.explanation: Thesis Two opens a space of non-belonging distinct from enmity.

lessons.title: Not kin, neighbor, citizen or friend
lessons.description: Dean defines the comrade by contrast. It is not a blood relation, not a spatial one, not mediated by the state, and not the chosen preference of friendship.
objectives: Contrast the comrade with kin, neighbor and citizen
Explain why comrades are not friends and why the difference takes work
Explain the ‘inhuman’, generic dimension of the comrade

sections.heading: Not kin, not neighbor
paragraphs: One isn’t born a comrade. Kin can oppose each other politically; spouses need not be comrades (Frida Kahlo said Diego Rivera would never be anyone’s husband but was a great comrade). Mary Davis writes that comradeship builds on fraternity but transcends it: ‘brother’ and ‘sister’ assign gender and carry family rivalry, while comrade denotes flat equality and the desire not to let down or be let down. In Chevengur, the fatherless insist they are comrades, not brothers—families are stuck with each other, comrades need each other.

Nor is the comrade a neighbor. Proximity creates no comradeship; communists were suspected precisely because their ties could be tighter with distant comrades than with those next door. And ‘love thy comrade as thyself’ makes no sense: the comrade is not Žižek’s abyssal Other but a symbolic identity of those on the same side.

sections.heading: Not citizen, not friend
paragraphs: Citizenship is mediated by the state and territory; comradeship exceeds both. The state fears communists as people loyal to an organization that may aim to overthrow it, and comradeship unsettles the state’s practical identification of friend and enemy.

Friendship, after Aristotle and Derrida, is a chosen relation between few individuals, for their own good. Comradeship is intrinsically political and broad; one doesn’t choose one’s comrades—the collective does, through organization. Claudio Lomnitz shows how personal dislike and suspicion of treason blurred among Mexican revolutionaries; keeping friend and comrade distinct takes work. When Wilderson called his white comrade Trevor his best friend, Trevor replied that he had only comrades.
sections.callout: Families are stuck with each other; comrades need each other; friends choose each other.

sections.heading: The inhuman comrade
paragraphs: Comradeship abstracts from the person to ask what each can contribute to collective work. McCarthy-era anticommunists saw communists as robots, cogs and slaves—all the same. Dean reads this hyperbole as registering a truth: the comrade is generic, a disciplined relation exceeding personal interest.

The ‘other relations’ index degenerations: when comradeship is substantialized as race, nation or personality, the cut of the generic is lost. The fascist camerata and the military Kamerad cannot say that anyone can be a comrade, which is why Italian leftists say compagno and German socialists Genosse.

example.title: Work it through: the Relations lab
example.body: Pick a relation in the Relations lab and compare what mediates it: blood, place, the state, personal preference, or fidelity to a political truth. Then check which ones allow ‘anyone but not everyone’. Only the comrade combines openness to strangers with a political division.

lessons.distinction: Dean is not saying comrades cannot be friends, lovers or family. She says these relations differ in kind, may coexist, and must be kept distinct—because personal dislike is not political betrayal, and personal affection is not political agreement.

furtherReading.label: Marx · Instructions for the Delegates of the Provisional General Council (1866)

quiz.question: Who chooses one’s comrades, according to Dean?
options: Each individual, on the basis of virtue
The collective, through political organization
The state
Nobody; comrades are born
quiz.explanation: One doesn’t choose one’s comrades; choosing and counting are matters of organization.

quiz.question: How does Dean read the McCarthy-era claim that all communists were robots?
options: As hyperbole that registers a truth: the comrade is generic, a disciplined relation exceeding personal interest
As completely accurate
As irrelevant propaganda with no connection to comradeship
As proof that communists lacked judgment
quiz.explanation: The truth under the caricature is the comrade’s genericity.

lessons.title: Thesis Three: the individual as Other
lessons.description: Comrade names a relation, not an identity. Masks, interchangeability and Brecht’s The Measures Taken show the individual as locus of identity to be the comrade’s Other.
objectives: State Thesis Three
Explain the role of masks and fungibility
Distinguish the comrade from the militant and answer the ‘instrumentalism’ objection

sections.heading: Identity vanishes
paragraphs: A 1925 Pravda obituary praised a comrade for having no personal biography. Comrade attaches to a proper name but asserts a sameness, replacing ‘Sir’, ‘Madam’ and ‘Citizen’. A comrade of Dean’s once said after a demonstration that they didn’t even need each other’s names. At the same time, the address makes a cut: are you with us or not?
Oxana Timofeeva points to Bolshevik disguises: anyone could be under that mustache. Cold War officials complained that communists could not be spotted, since anyone could be one.

sections.heading: Masks, fungibility, militants
paragraphs: In Brecht’s The Measures Taken, agitators wear masks to work among Chinese workers, becoming empty pages for the revolution. A young comrade, moved by misery that cannot wait, tears off his mask, acts on his own judgment and endangers the work; identifiable, he agrees to be killed. Dean uses the play to show the antagonism between individual identity and comradeship.

Comrades are multiple and replaceable, elements of a collective—like the roommates and travelling companions of the word’s origins. This distinguishes the comrade from the militant, a single figure of political intensity whose label says nothing about relations with others. Post-1991 Russia even fought an etymological war over tovar to mock comradeship as a market relation.
sections.callout: Thesis Three: the individual as a locus of identity is the Other of the comrade.

sections.heading: Instrumental—and intimate
paragraphs: Anticommunists find it horrifying that comrade relations are means to an end. Dean replies that politics aims at ends beyond the individual and requires coordination; the objection presumes a totalizing politics rather than an abstract one, and shrinks meaning to self-relation.

She rejects the bourgeois fiction that intimacy depends on personal disclosure. There are intimacies of common work: preparing the paper, painting banners, planning an action, knocking on doors. A former CPUSA member described that life as intense and absorbing, full of a comradeship he never expected to know again.

example.title: Work it through: the leaflet team
example.body: Five people leaflet a train station at 6 a.m. It doesn’t matter who hands out which leaflet; any of them could swap places, and none needs to know the others’ life stories. Yet over months they become close in a particular way—through the work. That is Dean’s ‘intimacy of common work’.

lessons.distinction: The Measures Taken is a deliberately harsh, much-debated play; Dean uses it to illustrate a structure, not to endorse killing dissenters. Critics worry that ‘the individual as Other’ licenses the suppression of judgment. Dean’s own chapter four shows how discipline can turn destructive—read the two together.

furtherReading.label: Dean · Four Theses on the Comrade (e-flux, 2017)

quiz.question: How does Dean distinguish the comrade from the militant?
options: The militant is always armed
The comrade is a leader, the militant a follower
The militant expresses political intensity as a single figure; the comrade names a relation among many
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: ‘Militant’ tells us nothing about relations with others; ‘comrade’ is relational.

quiz.question: What is Dean’s answer to the charge that comrade relations are merely instrumental?
options: She agrees that comradeship is immoral
She says comrades are friends first
She denies that comrades have goals
Political work aims beyond the individual and needs coordination; there are real intimacies of common work
quiz.explanation: She rejects the fiction that only personal disclosure produces intimacy.

lessons.title: Thesis Four: fidelity to a truth
lessons.description: What makes comrades the same is not identity but fidelity to a political truth, materialized in practice and organized in a party. Dean builds the thesis from Marx and Badiou.
objectives: Trace ‘comrade’ in nineteenth-century socialism and in Marx
Explain Badiou’s notions of event, truth and fidelity
Explain why Dean replaces Badiou’s militant with the comrade and the party as body

sections.heading: Party comrades
paragraphs: By the 1880s ‘comrade’ was common among English socialists inspired by Whitman, who wanted more than brotherhood or fraternity. One early US socialist preferred Whitman’s ‘comrade’ to the International’s ‘Citizen’. But the word was already part of German socialist vocabulary.

Marx praised ‘our heroic Party comrades in Paris’—party in the broad historical sense of those on the side of the people’s revolution—and in 1866 hoped the International would make workers of different countries act as comrades in the army of emancipation. Pabst’s film Kameradschaft (1931) shows French and German miners rescuing each other across a border.

sections.heading: Event, truth, fidelity
paragraphs: Badiou treats truth as a process. It begins with an event that breaks the given situation and cannot be decided in its terms. A subject is the response that decides the event took place, and fidelity is the work of verifying and extending its consequences in the world—in politics, a struggle of the many.

Peter Hallward stresses that fidelity is subjective, ex-centric and anti-private: one matters only as part of an impersonal vector, such as a political organization. Collectivity does not mean uniformity; verification involves many experiments.

sections.heading: Comrade, not militant; party as body
paragraphs: Badiou says the immediate subject of an organization is the political militant. Dean amends this: the comrade, because fidelity cannot be exercised alone. Drawing on Badiou’s earlier Theory of the Subject, she calls the party the body of politics—for a subject to be found, there must be the support of a body.

Comrades are a faithful response to the egalitarian rupture of crowds, a relation faithful to the divided people as subject. In Ninotchka it isn’t the greeting that makes the four comrades but membership of the same party, which mediates their relation and makes clear what is expected: disciplined, faithful work. No one is a comrade on their own.
sections.callout: Thesis Four: comrades are bound by fidelity to a truth, made real through organized, common practice.

example.title: Work it through: after the uprising
example.body: A mass protest erupts after a police killing. Many people are moved; some go home and post about it. Others form neighbourhood committees, keep meeting, and build a campaign that lasts years. In Dean’s Badiouian terms, the second group shows fidelity: they decide the event mattered and work out its consequences together, in an organized body.

lessons.distinction: ‘Truth’ here does not mean a correct proposition or a dogma believed on faith. It names a process opened by an event and sustained by practice. Dean also departs from Badiou—who distrusts parties—by giving fidelity a party as its body. Readers of Badiou dispute whether that move is faithful to him.

furtherReading.label: Marx · Letter to Kugelmann on the Paris Commune (1871)

quiz.question: Why does Dean replace Badiou’s ‘political militant’ with the comrade?
options: Because political fidelity cannot be exercised by a solitary individual
Because militants are violent
Because Badiou never wrote about militants
Because the comrade is a more heroic figure
quiz.explanation: ‘Comrade’ highlights the discipline of the event and the collective character of fidelity.

quiz.question: In Dean’s reading of Ninotchka, what makes the four characters comrades?
options: Calling each other ‘comrade’
Being Russian
Membership of the same party, which mediates their relation and sets expectations
Personal friendship
quiz.explanation: The address alone does not do it; the party as organized body of truth does.

lessons.title: Discipline, joy, enthusiasm, courage
lessons.description: Four attributes follow from the four theses. Dean defends discipline as the language of collective desire—then admits its superegoic danger and argues against Žižek for a politics with a body.
objectives: Define each of the four attributes of the comrade
Explain why discipline is liberating and how it can become superegoic
Summarize Dean’s objection to Žižek’s ‘four concepts’

sections.heading: Discipline and joy
paragraphs: If communism is a collective desire for collectivity, discipline is its law and language: meetings, reports, campaigns, unity in action turn scattered longing into collective will, and planning keeps desire alive. Lenin saw freely accepted discipline as a victory over one’s own egoism and habits; Orwell said revolutionary discipline depends on understanding why an order must be obeyed.

Joy accompanies discipline. Lenin quoted a Pravda report on a subbotnik where railway workers rolled a huge locomotive tyre into place and finished by singing the Internationale. Collective discipline lets comrades do what seemed impossible; joy testifies to the freedom discipline affords.

sections.heading: Enthusiasm and courage
paragraphs: Enthusiasm is the surplus energy collective work produces: because comrades combine forces they generate more than each alone. Raphael Samuel remembered the Communist Party of Great Britain as full of people whose energy set an example. Lenin praised it in What Is to Be Done? and in women comrades.

Courage is not an individual virtue but an effect of discipline—Liu Shaoqi’s communist, without selfish motives, has nothing to fear and can admit mistakes. It includes self-criticism, steadfastness under hardship, and, in Kollontai’s portraits of women of October, holding firm when stronger comrades wavered.
sections.callout: Discipline, joy, enthusiasm, courage: the comrade’s practical fidelity.

sections.heading: A politics with a body—and its dangers
paragraphs: Žižek proposes anxiety, courage, terror and enthusiasm as fundamental concepts of emancipatory politics. Dean’s objection: this politics has no body. It describes the atmosphere of revolution but lacks the organized form needed for fidelity and endurance. The party’s four concepts—concentration, endurance, fidelity, transference—yield, in its members, discipline, joy, enthusiasm and courage.

Dean admits discipline carries all the excesses of the superego. Trotsky called the crushed Kronstadt rebels ‘comrades’, and betrayal by comrades fuels particular fury; the party’s attacks on itself often exceeded its attacks on others. When the demand to do more becomes impossible purity, expulsions multiply and comrades become their own worst enemies. Her advantage, she says, is shifting the focus from terror inflicted on others to the sacrifices politics asks of those who undertake it.

example.title: Work it through: the Discipline lab
example.body: Move the discipline slider in the lab. At first, shared expectations raise capacity, joy and courage. Past a point, the model adds superegoic excess—fear, purges, burnout—and capacity falls. It is a caricature, but it captures Dean’s double claim: discipline is what makes a collective strong, and the same discipline can destroy what it built.

lessons.distinction: Dean’s defence of discipline is a central point of disagreement among her readers. Some find it a needed corrective to left individualism; others fear it rehabilitates authoritarian party practices. Note that she herself names the superego’s excess and devotes chapter four to its damage—her claim is not that discipline is safe, but that politics without it has no body.

quiz.question: What is Dean’s main objection to Žižek’s four concepts (anxiety, courage, terror, enthusiasm)?
options: They are too optimistic
They ignore anxiety
They are borrowed from Kant
That politics has no body: it lacks organized form for fidelity and endurance
quiz.explanation: His concepts describe revolution’s atmosphere but lack political form.

quiz.question: How does Dean describe enthusiasm?
options: A personal temperament some comrades happen to have
The surplus energy that collective, disciplined work generates
The opposite of discipline
A dangerous emotion to be suppressed
quiz.explanation: Combined forces generate more than each alone; enthusiasm is that surplus.

lessons.title: Expulsion, resignation, drift
lessons.description: How does comradeship end? Dean studies expulsion through the 1931 Yokinen trial and the later ‘phony war’, resignation through C. L. R. James and others, and the quiet end of drift.
objectives: Explain why Dean refuses to let fear of failure block a beginning
Contrast the Yokinen trial with the ‘phony war’ against white chauvinism
Distinguish expulsion, resignation and drift

sections.heading: ‘I have a comrade’
paragraphs: No one says ‘I am a comrade’ as people say ‘I am an ally’; the word points to someone else who stands with me. Discipline, Dean argues, also relieves: with comrades we need not know and do everything alone, react to every outrage or hide behind cynicism; when we err, comrades catch us. Exhausted people sometimes want to be told what to do.

To the left’s many ‘buts’—betrayal, failure, harm, persisting bigotry—Dean answers that rejecting a beginning because it might end is a failure of will. She studies four endings: expulsion, resignation, drift and the end of the world.

sections.heading: Expulsion: Yokinen and the phony war
paragraphs: Beyond the Bolshevik expulsions, Dean focuses on Harlem, 1931. August Yokinen, a Finnish worker, had failed to defend black workers driven out of a club dance. Before 1,500 people and a jury of seven black and seven white workers, Clarence Hathaway argued for expulsion; Richard B. Moore’s defence argued that capitalism and the party’s own failures were also on trial and urged self-criticism. Yokinen was expelled with a path back—and, arrested for deportation the next day, was defended by the party. Haywood saw this as correct practice of rectification.

In the early 1950s, under McCarthyist pressure and after the party had dropped self-determination, Haywood describes a ‘phony war’ against chauvinism: a moral crusade cut off from mass work, measured by the number of disciplinary actions. Comrades feared visiting each other; whole branches were liquidated. The expelled faced social death—‘nonassociation’, as Jessica Mitford recalled.

sections.heading: Resignation and drift
paragraphs: Resignation happens when a comrade sees they are no longer on the same side. C. L. R. James left Correspondence in 1962, declaring those who make the fundamentals of Marxism negotiable to be enemies, friends those drawn to resist capitalism, comrades those who share the cause. Other resignations are acts of comradeship: party members who quit to give money to Junius Scales’s family, or Queen Mother Moore leaving when the party would not discuss its retreat from self-determination—fear, she found, had replaced courage.

Drift is quieter: the heart leaks out; a dues collector simply stops coming. Lillian Hellman drifted because she always valued independence. And commanding people to say ‘comrade’, as the Chinese party has, cannot stop drift: a comrade who is your superior on a ladder is no comrade.
sections.callout: Expelled, but given a path back: Dean’s model of an ending that keeps comradeship alive.

example.title: Work it through: two disciplinary meetings
example.body: An organizer makes a racist remark. Meeting A: a public hearing, clear explanation of why it harms the struggle, concrete tasks to make amends, a defined route back. Meeting B: anonymous accusations, a purity test, permanent exclusion, and silence from former friends. Dean’s chapter asks you to see why A strengthens the side and B dissolves it.

lessons.distinction: Dean reads these episodes as lessons, not verdicts on communism as a whole. She takes Haywood’s side on the ‘phony war’, but also quotes Paul Jarrico, who thought the fight against white chauvinism was among the few things the party got clearly right. Keep these perspectives distinct.

quiz.question: What distinguished the Yokinen expulsion, in Dean’s and Haywood’s view?
options: It was a path of rectification: expelled with concrete tasks and a route back, and defended against deportation
It ended his comradeship forever
It was secret
Yokinen was found innocent
quiz.explanation: Expulsion was a moment, not a banishment; the party kept him in the struggle.

quiz.question: Why, for Dean, can’t commanding the use of ‘comrade’ stop drift?
options: Because the word is too old-fashioned
Because party members don’t understand it
Because the word is banned

quiz.explanation: Compelled address can signal that comradeship is already absent.

lessons.title: The end of the world—and reading Dean critically
lessons.eyebrow: Chapter Four · The End of the World · §§62–64
lessons.description: Lessing’s The Golden Notebook shows comradeship ending as the collapse of a shared language. Dean closes with comrades after communism—then we weigh the book’s main criticisms.
objectives: Explain why Dean calls the collapse of the party the end of a world
Interpret the ‘I, I, I’ and the loss of shared meaning
Evaluate the main objections to Comrade

sections.heading: Words lose their meaning
paragraphs: Doris Lessing’s 1962 novel follows Anna Wulf after 1956: Khrushchev’s speech, Hungary, Suez. Anna keeps separate notebooks to ward off chaos. She joins the party drawn by the atmosphere of people working for a common end, yet tells her therapist she cannot say ‘we’ and mean it. In a writers’ group, words begin to sound foreign, and she starts to stammer.

For Dean, unlike drift—where the communist symbolic world continues without you—this is the collapse of the symbolic order itself. Molly no longer cares; her son Tommy shoots himself and survives blind; Anna and Saul call each other ‘comrade’ with ironic nostalgia while Saul’s speech dissolves into ‘I, I, I’. Collapse and capitalism—Dean calls this our setting of survivors and systems.

sections.heading: Comrades after communism?
paragraphs: The novel ends in private life: Tommy joins his father’s business, Molly remarries, Anna becomes a marriage counsellor. Dean hears Thatcher’s ‘no such thing as society’ coming: losing the party means losing a perspective from which society can be seen. That is the world after 1956, 1968 and 1989.

Asked whether there will be comrades after communism, Dean answers that communism is not the end of history but its condition of possibility. Comradeship is not risk-free or magic, but it is the only form through which the left’s problems can be solved. The question itself, coming from a comrade, presupposes victory.
sections.callout: To be a left at all, Dean concludes, we have to be comrades.

sections.heading: Reading Comrade critically
paragraphs: Several objections are worth weighing. The archive is narrow—mostly the CPUSA of the 1920s–50s—and selective, sometimes treating Soviet-aligned party history more generously than many historians. Its critique of allyship targets popular online guides rather than the strongest work on solidarity, coalition and intersectionality, much of which also stresses collective organizing.

Others worry that genericity can hide who gets to define the ‘side’, and that the praise of discipline underestimates the abuses of party hierarchies—though Dean names the superego’s excesses herself. Defenders answer that the book is an essay, not a history, aimed at a left that has lost the habit of organized belonging. A good reading keeps her claims, her examples and her critics apart.

example.title: Work it through: test a claim
example.body: Choose one of Dean’s claims—say, that allyship is a symptom of politics shrinking into self-help. Find one example that supports it (a viral list of ‘ally dos and don’ts’) and one that challenges it (a coalition where self-described allies organized strikes or tenant unions). Ask what each example shows about form: individual attitude, or collective organization?

lessons.distinction: Three voices should stay separate: what Lessing’s novel shows, what Dean argues it shows, and what critics say about Dean. The Golden Notebook has many readings—feminist, formal, psychological as well as political. Dean uses it as a figure for the end of a shared world, not as a full interpretation of the novel.
