quiz.question: How does Dean distinguish ‘the end of the world’ from drift?
options: Drift is violent, the end of the world is quiet
There is no difference
In drift the communist symbolic world continues without you; in Lessing the shared symbolic order itself collapses
Drift happens to leaders, the end of the world to members
quiz.explanation: Words lose their meaning; the common language that made ‘we’ possible dissolves.

quiz.question: What is Dean’s answer to the question of whether there will be comrades after communism?
options: No—once there are no sides, comrades disappear
Communism is history’s condition of possibility, not its end; the question presupposes victory and desires the comrade relation
Yes—everyone will automatically be a comrade
The question cannot be asked
quiz.explanation: She reframes communism as the condition for a future, and hears the question as a comrade’s hope.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s generic figure for the political relation between those on the same side of a struggle—at once a term of address, a figure of belonging and a carrier of expectations.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It names a relation, not a type of person; one would not say ‘I am a comrade’.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s image, from camera (room, vault), for what comradeship provides: a space held open that separates an inside from an outside and shelters those within.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A structural metaphor, not a demand for physical closeness.

glossaryTerms.definition: The ground of comradeship: sameness with respect to a political division, regardless of individual differences.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Sameness of side, not uniformity of persons or opinions.

glossaryTerms.definition: ‘Comrade’ used to hail someone, replacing titles like ‘Sir’ or ‘Citizen’; it equalizes and also reminds the addressee of what is expected.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Address alone does not make comrades; the party and practice do (Thesis Four).

glossaryTerms.definition: The comrade as a bundle of shared expectations for action—show up, don’t distance yourself, do the work.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Without expectations of solidarity, ‘comrade’ becomes an ironic or nostalgic gesture.

glossaryTerms.definition: Seeing your own actions through your comrades’ eyes; the reason people do political work they would otherwise avoid.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not surveillance by a superior but a perspective produced by shared commitment.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thesis Two: comradeship is open to anyone, but presupposes a division, so not everyone is a comrade.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not-comrade does not mean enemy; there is a space of bystanders, allies and future comrades.

glossaryTerms.definition: Lacan’s term for a ‘feminine’ structure without a founding exception; Dean applies it to comrade as anyone-but-not-everyone.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It describes a logical structure, not women or femininity as such.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s name for a tendency on the left to cling to identities forged in struggles to survive, often attached to their pain.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A critique of a political frame, not a denial that people have survived real harm.

glossaryTerms.definition: The opposite tendency: fascination with vast processes—extinction, algorithms, hyperobjects—that seem beyond any human agency.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean’s objection is to the disappearance of collective agency, not to studying systems.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s term for capitalism intensified through networked, personalized digital media, where circulation and number dominate.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It describes a structure of circulation, not just ‘social media’.

glossaryTerms.definition: The neoliberal subject treated as the locus of autonomous choices while facing conditions outside its control.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The other pole of this split is impersonal systems; together they displace politics.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s openings for politics today: the power of number, identity’s declining grip, generic markers, and movements hitting the limits of horizontality.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Openings, not guarantees—each requires organization to become political.

glossaryTerms.definition: Shared symbols such as hashtags and memes that carry many particular contents and let local struggles see themselves as part of something larger.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A first, thin form of the generic; the comrade is a stronger one.

glossaryTerms.definition: Identities are split and contested sites of class struggle, not grounds from which politics follows automatically.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean does not say identities are unreal, only that they decide nothing politically.

glossaryTerms.definition: The model of politics in which privileged individuals help the oppressed through self-work; Dean reads it as a symptom of politics shrinking.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: She rejects allyship as a model, not tactical alliances.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s phrase for a culture where people can be scolded and shamed but no one is responsible for guidance or collective training.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The contrast is with comradely discipline, which includes support and correction.

glossaryTerms.definition: Communism as the horizon of left politics: negatively, the negation of global capitalism; positively, production organized around social needs by the producers.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A horizon orients struggle; it is not a blueprint.

glossaryTerms.definition: Bernard Aspe’s term, used by Dean, for time generated and enjoyed in collective being-together, against time enclosed for capitalist appropriation.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Not leisure as such—shared time outside capitalist measurement.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s approach in chapter two: lifting examples out of their historical contexts and salvaging them for present struggles.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It is not a full history; check her examples against historians.

glossaryTerms.definition: The theory, developed by Louise Thompson Patterson and Claudia Jones, that black women are exploited as workers, as women and as black people.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: A communist theory decades before ‘intersectionality’ was coined.

glossaryTerms.definition: The 1940s dispute over Mary Inman’s claim that housework is productive labour; the CPUSA rejected it but treated her as a comrade.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean contests the later story that the party ignored women’s oppression.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cyril Briggs’s test of white solidarity: willingness to accept black armed self-defence, even against white people.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It measures commitment under cost, not sympathy.

glossaryTerms.definition: The CPUSA expectation that comradeship extend into everyday personal relations across the colour line.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Often unmet in practice, as Claudia Jones charged in 1949.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Comintern/CPUSA line (from 1928) that black people in the Southern Black Belt formed an oppressed nation with a right to self-determination.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean defends its political function, not every element of its 1928 formulation.

glossaryTerms.definition: The CPUSA’s term for racism among white workers and party members, which it campaigned to root out.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: The campaign could be real struggle or a ‘phony war’ cut off from mass work (chapter four).

glossaryTerms.definition: Russian for ‘others’ or ‘miscellaneous’; in Platonov’s Chevengur, the classless, propertyless people who have only each other.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean reads them as the zero-level of comradeship, not as an ideal.

glossaryTerms.definition: German and Russian words for comrade: one linked to shared enjoyment, the other to tovar, commodity.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean resolves the contrast as the collective self-possession of the unpropertied.

glossaryTerms.definition: Chinese for comrade; in contemporary usage also ‘gay’. Hongwei Bao calls it intrinsically queer.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It shows comrade opening kinship to strangers who share a politics.

glossaryTerms.definition: The comrade as the minimal relation remaining when property, class and identity are gone—the starting point for something new.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Visible only retroactively, from a political project, not in destitution as such.

glossaryTerms.definition: Comrade names a relation of sameness, equality and solidarity; for communists it is utopian, cutting through capitalist determinations.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Utopian here means estranging and hopeful, not naive.

glossaryTerms.definition: The individual as a locus of identity is the comrade’s Other.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: It targets identity as the basis of belonging, not the existence of persons.

glossaryTerms.definition: The relation between comrades is mediated by fidelity to a truth; practices of comradeship build that truth into the world.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Truth as a process (Badiou), not a dogma.

glossaryTerms.definition: Indifferent to individual specificity; a form that can contain any content. Dean’s comrade is generic, not unique.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Generic is not the same as universal: not everyone is a comrade.

glossaryTerms.definition: A single figure of political intensity; unlike the comrade, the term says nothing about relations with others.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean replaces Badiou’s militant with the comrade.

glossaryTerms.definition: The symbolic point from which one observes and judges oneself; Dean’s main sense of the comrade.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Don’t confuse with the ideal ego, the imaginary self-image.

glossaryTerms.definition: The imaginary image of who one would like to be—the brilliant orator, the fearless militant. Dean places the ally here.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Imaginary, not symbolic: it flatters rather than judges.

glossaryTerms.definition: Badiou’s account of truth as a process opened by an event and sustained by faithful, collective work on its consequences.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean adds a body: the party.

glossaryTerms.definition: The idea, from Badiou’s Theory of the Subject, that for a political subject to be found there must be an organized body—Dean’s party.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: ‘Party’ in both the formal and the broad historical sense.

glossaryTerms.definition: The punishing agency that demands ever more; Dean’s name for the danger in discipline when it turns into purges and impossible purity.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Discipline can be creative or destructive; the superego names the second turn.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freely accepted collective expectations—meetings, tasks, unity in action—that turn individual longing into collective will.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Dean treats it as liberating and dangerous at once.

glossaryTerms.definition: With discipline, the four attributes of the comrade: the felt freedom of collective work, its surplus energy, and steadfastness born of shared commitment.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Courage is an effect of discipline, not an individual virtue.

glossaryTerms.definition: The party’s declaration that comradeship has ended; in the Yokinen trial, a moment with a path back rather than a banishment.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Compare the 1950s ‘phony war’, where expulsions ran amok.

glossaryTerms.definition: Haywood’s term for correcting errors while keeping the comrade in the struggle.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Its opposite is social death through ‘nonassociation’.

glossaryTerms.definition: The quiet end of comradeship: diminishing attachment until someone simply stops coming.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Compelling people to use the word ‘comrade’ cannot stop it.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dean’s reading of The Golden Notebook: the end of comradeship as the collapse of a shared language and symbolic order.
glossaryTerms.watchFor: Unlike drift, the world itself—not just one’s place in it—dissolves.
